newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Army expects more charges in rape scandal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Army expects more charges in rape scandal.

text.p: The Army said on Friday it expected to charge more people as it rapidly addressed a scandal involving alleged rape of female recruits at this training base.

"I would expect additional charges to be coming," Maj. Gen. Robert Shadley told reporters. He would not elaborate, but choked back emotion at a news conference, calling the military's latest harassment case "absolutely deplorable.

"We as leaders have a responsibility to take care of our soldiers and it breaks your heart when we don't," said Shadley, commander of the Army Ordnance and Doctrine Command's training facility here at Aberdeen near Baltimore.
"We want those individuals out in front of our soldiers in formation or in front of them in a classroom to be leaders and not lechers," he said.

The Army said on Thursday that three male trainers, including two drill instructors, had been charged in connection with allegations of coerced sex and harassment involving at least 17 women at the base, where newly enlisted young men and women are taught Army skills.
"We have no evidence of a conspiracy," said Shadley, adding that investigators were contacting up to 1,000 women who passed through the ordnance centre and school in a hunt for possible victims.
Civilian Army Secretary Togo West said every woman who came to the facility as a trainee since the start of 1995 would be asked about her experiences.

West told PBS-TV's "NewsHour with Jim Lehrer" the Pentagon was conducting an internal investigation of all training bases "to understand the climate and whether there is something here we've missed ... We think it's not the ingrained culture. We hope it's not."
West said he was appointing a panel of experts, from inside and outside the Army, to review all Army operations and determine if similar abuses were occurring at other facilities.

The Pentagon fears that the scandal will give the U.S. military another black eye in a string of harassment cases that began with the 1991 "Tailhook" scandal in which male Navy and Marine pilots fondled women at a Las Vegas hotel.
The three men already charged, including a captain who was a company commander, helped train hundreds of young recruits in tasks from handling ammunition to repairing trucks at Aberdeen.
Those charged so far include Sgt. Delmar Simpson, jailed on charges including rape, sodomy, adultery and obstruction of justice and illegal fraternisation with recruits.
Capt. Derrick Robertson, charged with rape, adultery and conduct unbecoming an officer as well as fraternisation, has been relieved of duty pending further investigation.
Staff Sgt. Nathanial Beach has been charged with disobeying an order, obstruction of justice and fraternisation.
Shadley said some 550 women had already been interviewed by investigators and that the alleged victims in the case were cooperating extensively.
Army lawyers said conviction of rape in the service is punishable by penalties that can range up to life in prison.

The Defence Department, which has mandated "sensitivity" training for all personnel since "Tailhook" and has stressed promotion of women to higher rank, reported in July that sexual harassment in the military had declined slightly.
The Army chief of staff, Gen. Dennis Reimer, and West expressed shock on Thursday over the latest scandal and said all Army personnel would be ordered to undergo renewed sexual harassment training.
